approach: The authors conducted a narrative review by synthesizing data from various clinical trials (Phase I-III), retrospective and prospective observational studies, and meta-analyses. They organized the literature into specific categories of biomarkers (biochemical, cellular, tumor-related, imaging, etiological, microbiome, and safety-related) and summarized their predictive value for outcomes such as overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), and disease control rate (DCR).

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a comprehensive categorization of diverse biomarkers (serum, cellular, tumor, host, microbiome) for ICI efficacy in HCC, serving as a reference for clinical trial design and biomarker discovery.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Most included studies are retrospective with small sample sizes; lack of standardized protocols for novel biomarkers (ctDNA, microbiome); conflicting results for several markers (PD-L1, TMB, antibiotics); insufficient prospective validation for many candidates.

key_findings.finding: Low baseline AFP (<400 µg/L) and low CRAFITY score (combining AFP and CRP) are associated with better OS and PFS. Low ALBI score indicates preserved liver function and predicts better survival. High IL-6 and TGF-b levels correlate with poor response.
Low NLR (<5), low PLR, high PNI, and low MLR/CII/SIRI are generally associated with improved OS and PFS. Early changes in monocyte subsets (e.g., CD14+/CD16+) also show predictive potential.

PD-L1 expression shows inconsistent predictive value in HCC. TMB has limited utility due to low mutation burden in HCC. ctDNA clearance and low baseline cfDNA levels correlate with better outcomes. CTCs with PD-L1 expression have conflicting results regarding response prediction.

Splenomegaly and sarcopenia (low SMI) are associated with poorer prognosis. Older age (≥65 years) may respond better to ICIs. HBV-related HCC tends to have better outcomes than non-viral or HCV-related HCC. NASH-related HCC shows poorer response.

Specific microbial compositions (e.g., enrichment of Lachnoclostridium, Veillonella; absence of Prevotella 9) correlate with better response. Antibiotic use during treatment is associated with shorter PFS and OS in some studies, though results are conflicting.
Some studies suggest irAEs (especially grade ≥3) correlate with better survival, but other large studies found no significant difference. CRAFITY score may predict lower incidence of severe irAEs.

problem_or_question: To identify reliable prognostic biomarkers that can predict the efficacy of ICIs treatment in HCC patients, thereby enabling optimal patient selection to maximize clinical benefits while minimizing unnecessary toxic side effects and economic losses.
research_scope: Advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 agents, often in combination with targeted therapies or other modalities.
work_summary: This review systematically categorizes and summarizes current evidence on biomarkers predicting the efficacy of ICIs in HCC. It covers a wide range of indicators including serum/cellular markers (e.g., AFP, ALBI, NLR, cytokines), tumor-related markers (e.g., PD-L1, TMB, ctDNA, CTCs), clinical/imaging features (e.g., splenomegaly, sarcopenia, BMI), etiology (HBV/HCV/NASH), gut microbiome, and immune-related adverse events (irAEs). The paper aims to guide future biomarker exploration and clinical decision-making by highlighting promising candidates and identifying areas requiring further validation through larger prospective studies.
